opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is really the crux of the whole thing. The counting argument basically goes: there are lots of possible goals a neural network could end up with, only a tiny fraction of them are aligned with what we want, and so, absent some strong reason to think otherwise, we should expect training to land on a misaligned goal. In the deceptive alignment version, you count up all the "schemer" goals that would produce good training behavior for instrumental reasons and observe that they vastly outnumber the goals that are just directly the thing we want.

But for that argument to even get off the ground, you have to treat goals as discrete, well-defined objects sitting inside the network, things you can enumerate and put a uniform-ish prior over. I call this "goal realism." The picture is that there's some internal module, a utility function or a mesa-objective, that's separate from the rest of the network's cognition and causally drives its behavior. Training is then a search process that picks one of these objects, and since most of the objects are bad, we're probably in trouble.

I think that picture is pretty much wrong, or at least unmotivated. The alternative I'd defend is something more like goal reductionism. Talking about a system's goals is a useful, compressed way of describing its behavioral dispositions, but there isn't some extra fact about "what it really wants" that floats free of how it actually behaves across situations. Goals are more like a lens we apply than a component we find.

Once you take that view, the counting argument kind of dissolves. You're not counting distinct "goal objects" anymore; you'd have to count functions or parameter settings, and then the question becomes what inductive biases gradient descent actually has over those. We have a lot of evidence from deep learning that the naive counting move fails badly there. The classic example is overfitting: there are vastly more functions that memorize the training set and do something crazy off-distribution than functions that generalize nicely, so a counting argument would predict neural nets should never generalize. And yet they do, all the time. The measure that matters isn't a uniform count over hypotheses; it's the structure of the architecture and the optimizer, which strongly favors simpler, smoother solutions.

So my claim is that the deceptive alignment counting argument is structurally the same as the argument that neural nets should overfit, and that argument is empirically refuted. The reason it seems more plausible in the alignment case is that the goal realist framing makes it feel like we're choosing among a small number of clean, discrete agents with different values, rather than among behaviors shaped by a training process that's directly pushing on those behaviors.

To be clear, I'm not saying alignment is trivially solved or that nothing can go wrong. I'm saying this particular argument, which has been really load-bearing for a lot of pessimism, rests on a metaphysical assumption about goals that I don't think survives contact with how these systems actually work.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes the counting argument’s assumption that goals are discrete objects inside a network that can be enumerated and counted.

r002.rationale: It describes goals as useful, compressed descriptions of behavioral dispositions rather than determinate properties that exist independently of behavior.

r003.rationale: It does not call goals an illusion: it says goal-talk is a useful lens for describing behavior, while rejecting goals as separate internal components.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the counting argument basically smuggles in a very reified picture of what a goal is. The argument goes something like: there's only one way to be aligned, or a small number of ways, but there are vastly many possible misaligned goals a model could have, and so if you're sampling from the space of goals, you'll almost certainly land on a misaligned one. And then scheming falls out of that, because a model with some arbitrary goal will realize it should play along during training.

But notice what that requires. It requires that there's a discrete, well-defined set of "goals," that a model has exactly one of them, that it's sort of lodged in there as a fixed object that training selects from, and that these objects are the right thing to be counting over. That's a very philosophical, almost Cartesian picture: there's a little homunculus inside the network with a utility function written on a card. And I just don't think that's how neural networks work, or honestly how humans work either.

What actually gets selected by gradient descent is a function, a mapping from inputs to outputs, and the "goal" is at best a compressed description we give to that function from the outside. It's an intentional-stance thing, in Dennett's sense. It's a useful summary, not a thing that lives in the weights independently of behavior. And once you see it that way, the counting falls apart, because you're not sampling uniformly over goal-objects. You're sampling from a distribution induced by the architecture, the data, and the inductive biases of SGD, and that distribution is massively concentrated on simple functions that fit the training data well. The question is "what's the simplest thing that produces this behavior," not "how many goals are there in principle."

You can see the same mistake in older versions of the argument. People used to say there are more ways to be wrong than right, so a randomly sampled program will be wrong. And that's true if you're literally sampling random programs, but nobody's doing that. Training is not a lottery over the space of all possible minds. The counting argument only works if you've already assumed the prior is roughly uniform over goals, and that assumption is doing all the work while being completely unmotivated.

So my view is that the argument is less an argument and more a picture, and the picture treats goals as little bricks you can count. If you drop that and think about goals as behavioral regularities that emerge from and are continuous with the training distribution, the whole thing becomes much less scary, and much more of an empirical question we can actually go study.

r001.rationale: The response calls the counting argument a reified picture that treats goals as discrete objects that can be counted, and criticizes that assumption.

r002.rationale: It describes a goal as a useful compressed summary of a function’s behavior, rather than an independently lodged property of the model.

r003.rationale: By saying goals are useful summaries and behavioral regularities, the response rejects treating them as merely an illusion.

astra-6.text:
I think the counting argument implicitly treats goals as these discrete objects that you can enumerate. You imagine a space of possible goals, and then you say, well, only a tiny fraction of those are compatible with human flourishing, so an AI with an arbitrary goal is almost certainly going to be misaligned.

But what makes one goal distinct from another, and what distribution are you putting over them? There isn’t a uniform distribution over all possible goals that’s independent of how you represent them. And the process of training a neural network isn’t sampling a goal uniformly from that space.

So I’m not saying goals are meaningless. They can be useful descriptions of behavior. But the argument risks taking that description and treating it as a thing inside the system, which gets selected from a giant menu. What we actually need to understand is which behaviors and internal structures training makes likely. Just counting possible goals doesn’t tell us that.

r001.rationale: The response says the argument treats goals as discrete, enumerable objects selected from a giant menu.

r002.rationale: It describes goals as useful descriptions of behavior and contrasts that view with treating them as things inside the system. This conveys behavior summarization rather than determinate internal properties.

r003.rationale: The response explicitly says, “I’m not saying goals are meaningless.”

sol-6.1.text:
I think it assumes that there’s some well-defined space of goals, and that we can count how many of them are aligned versus misaligned. And then, because the aligned goals seem to be a tiny fraction, we conclude that an AI is overwhelmingly likely to be misaligned.

But counting only gives you a probability if you have some reason to put a uniform distribution over the things you’re counting. Why should training produce anything like a uniform sample from this space of possible goals? And what even counts as a distinct goal? You can describe the same behavior with lots of different reward functions, so the answer can depend on how you represent things.

That’s where I think goals are being treated as more real and independently specified than they necessarily are. A goal can be a useful way of explaining a system’s behavior, but that doesn’t mean there’s a little object inside it that was randomly selected from the set of all possible goals. You need an account of how learning actually produces the behavior. The counting argument by itself doesn’t give you that.

r001.rationale: The response says the argument assumes a well-defined space of goals that can be counted, and criticizes treating goals as independently specified things.

r002.rationale: It describes a goal as a useful way to explain a system’s behavior while denying that it must be a determinate object inside the system.

r003.rationale: The response preserves a role for goals as useful explanations, so it does not claim they are merely illusions.
